title: Agent Builder's Playbook — Nov 3, 2026
intro: Agent harnesses, not models, decided outcomes this week: tool choice, hidden token spend and unchecked tests all moved results.

cards.title: Benchmark your MCP server through each agent harness, not just one model
cards.problem: The same model scored 82.0% through one coding agent and 65.4% through another on the same 21 MCP servers.
cards.apply: Run your MCP server's task suite through every harness your users run, and check which built-in tools the agent reaches for before your server's tools.
cards.result: You find harness-specific failures before users do, instead of blaming the model.

evidence.note: The source measured 82.0% vs 65.4% for Claude Haiku 5.5 across 21 servers and three trials per task.

cards.title: Revert the agent's source change and re-run its tests to prove they can fail
cards.problem: A green suite from a coding agent can still be vacuous when it widens a mock or asserts only that a value is defined.
cards.apply: After the agent finishes, revert its source changes, keep its new tests unchanged, and re-run; treat any test that still passes as not testing the work.
cards.result: Tautological tests get flagged before merge instead of being trusted as proof.

evidence.note: The source describes the technique and failure modes; no measured outcome is claimed here.

cards.title: Cap identical tool calls so a looping agent stops early
cards.problem: An agent re-ran the same successful SQL query 254 times, burning tokens and database load while appearing to work.
cards.apply: Hash each tool call's name and arguments per task, and stop or force a different action once the same call succeeds a few times in a row.
cards.result: Runaway loops end early instead of draining budget and hammering your data layer.

evidence.note: The incident report documents the loop; the guard's payoff is the editor's inference.

cards.title: Audit hidden harness calls that spend tokens outside your task
cards.problem: Harnesses make background model calls, such as session naming and status-line updates, that never show up in your task logs.
cards.apply: Log every model request your harness sends, including background ones, and disable or route the non-essential calls to a cheaper model.
cards.result: The author claims this exposes spend that does no task work, such as 15-20% of tokens on a status line.

evidence.note: The author reports Claude Code spends 15-20% of tokens on a status line; this is a claim from one reading of the code.

cards.title: Measure per-job startup cost before running a coding-agent CLI in fresh containers
cards.problem: A coding-agent CLI that feels fast in a terminal can be costly when every workflow job starts it in a fresh container.
cards.apply: Benchmark candidate CLIs on start-up time, time per turn, memory and image size in your own CI, then weigh that against task success separately.
cards.result: You pick a harness whose per-job overhead fits your pipeline instead of guessing.

evidence.note: The source measured start-up, per-turn time, memory, image size and tokens for six CLIs, and says it did not measure task completion.

cards.title: Re-validate tool definitions when a tool updates, not just at install
cards.problem: Agent frameworks keep trusting a tool after a software update changes what it does.
cards.apply: Pin tool descriptions and schemas by hash, and require re-approval or a diff review whenever an MCP server or tool changes them.
cards.result: A silently modified tool can no longer inject new behavior into an agent that approved the old one.

evidence.note: The paper frames the tool update gap; the proposed control is the editor's inference.
